title: Council Tax after moving in: who pays, student exemptions, single-person discounts and billing problems
summary: How to deal with Council Tax after moving into a rented home in England: finding the right council, registering, who normally pays and the exceptions for shared houses, full-time student exemptions and evidence, the 25% single-person discount, challenging a wrong bill, and closing the account when you move out. Not every student or shared household is automatically exempt. Checked on 16 November 2026.
content:
# Council Tax after moving in: who pays, student exemptions, single-person discounts and billing problems

Last updated: 2026-11-21

> **Checked on: 16 November 2026.** For tenants renting in **England**. Council Tax is a local tax on domestic property, collected by local councils. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-what-it-is) This is general information; your council decides how the rules apply to you.

## 1. Find the right council

- Enter your postcode in GOV.UK's "Find your local council" to find the council for your new address. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-find-council)
- Every home has a Council Tax band. You can check it on GOV.UK, and it is also shown on your bill. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-band-check)
- Check your tenancy agreement and the agent's written information first: some lets include Council Tax in the rent. If nothing says so, the household usually deals with it.

## 2. Registering and paying after you move in

- Soon after you move in, register with the council on its website: your new address, the date you moved in and who lives with you. Forms and requirements differ, so follow your council's instructions.
- If you are not sure whether you can get a discount or who should pay, contact your local council. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ask-council)
- Your bill shows how much you pay for the year, how it was worked out and the payment dates; the cost is usually split into 10 monthly payments. If you have trouble paying, contact the council straight away, for example to spread payments over 12 months. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ten-months)
- You can usually pay online, or pay cash with PayPoint and similar services at post offices, banks and shops; your bill lists other methods. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ways-to-pay)

## 3. Who normally pays

- Usually the person living in the property pays; sometimes the owner has to pay. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-liable-person)
- Spouses and partners who live together are jointly responsible for the bill. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-couples)
- **Exception for shared houses:** if the property is a house in multiple occupation (HMO), the owner is liable. You will usually be in an HMO if you live in a shared house, bedsit or hostel with 2 or more people who are not part of the same family. It can be hard to tell, so check with your local council if you are unsure. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-hmo)

## 4. Students

- Households where everyone is a full-time student do not have to pay Council Tax; if you still get a bill, you can apply for an exemption. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-students-exempt)
- According to GOV.UK, to count as a full-time student your course must last at least 1 year and involve at least 21 hours of study per week. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-full-time-definition)
- The council might ask for proof that you are a full-time student. You can ask your university or college for a certificate. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-student-certificate)
- **Sharing with non-students:** the property is not exempt and there will be a bill, but whoever is liable might get a discount. For example, if you share with one employed person, they will probably be liable for 75%. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-mixed-household)
- Between courses, for example after one course ends and before the next starts, you might have to pay Council Tax. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-between-courses)
- Not every student or shared household is automatically exempt. Whether an exemption or discount applies is decided by the council.

## 5. Single-person discount and people who are "disregarded"

- If you pay Council Tax and either live on your own or everyone else in your home is "disregarded", you get 25% off; if everyone in the household is disregarded, you get 50% off. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-discounts)
- You must apply for a discount or exemption, even if you are disregarded. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-must-apply)
- If you get a discount by mistake, you must tell the council, or you could get a fine. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-discount-mistake)

## 6. If your bill is wrong

- Tell your council immediately if you think your home should not be charged, the bill is going to the wrong person, the amount is wrong, or you have not been given a discount you should get. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-appeal-reasons)
- Write and explain why. The council has 2 months to reply, and you must keep paying the amounts on your original bill until a new bill arrives. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-appeal-process)
- If you disagree with the council's decision, or do not hear back within 2 months, you can appeal to the independent Valuation Tribunal; time limits apply. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-tribunal)
- You cannot appeal just because the bill seems too expensive. If you think the band is wrong, challenge it with the Valuation Office through the GOV.UK service. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-band-challenge)

## 7. When you move out

- Tell the council and the utility suppliers that you are leaving; pay the final bills and give your new address. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-leaving)
- If you have overpaid and have not had an automatic refund, contact your local council. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-overpaid)

## If the property is empty or you move across the UK
An empty property can still attract Council Tax in England. If you move out before your tenancy ends, give the council the date you left, when the tenancy ends and when you returned the keys. If you rent the whole property, you may still owe Council Tax until your tenancy ends. Ask the council to confirm the chargeable dates and whether any discount, exemption or premium applies. [Tenancy and unoccupied periods](#guide-evidence-tenancy-period) [England rules](#guide-evidence-empty-england)

Scotland and Wales have separate rules and council policies. Northern Ireland uses domestic rates: report moving to Land & Property Services. [Scotland](#guide-evidence-empty-scotland) · [Wales](#guide-evidence-empty-wales) · [Northern Ireland](#guide-evidence-ni-rates)

## Official and authoritative sources

- Citizens Advice — Check how council tax works and if you have to pay — https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/housing/council-tax/paying-council-tax/
- GOV.UK — Find your local council — https://www.gov.uk/find-local-council
- GOV.UK — Council Tax — https://www.gov.uk/council-tax
- Citizens Advice — Paying council tax if you're a student — https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/housing/council-tax/student-housing-council-tax/
- GOV.UK — Appeal a Council Tax bill or fine — https://www.gov.uk/council-tax-appeals
- GOV.UK — Check your Council Tax band — https://www.gov.uk/council-tax-bands
- Shelter England — What to do when you leave your private rented home — https://england.shelter.org.uk/housing_advice/private_renting/what_to_do_when_you_leave_your_rented_home

The sources above were accessed on 16 November 2026.

Last updated: 16 November 2026. This is general information, not legal or financial advice, and it has not been reviewed by a lawyer; if the rules change, GOV.UK, the relevant regulator and the relevant law take precedence. This Guide does not recommend any particular company or deal.
